449.title: Ignorance — mistaking the passing for the permanent (2.4–2.5)
449.hook: Patanjali defines the root of every affliction as four simple mix-ups, and the first is mistaking the passing for the permanent
449.howItsDone: In yoga and Vedanta teaching, avidya is treated as the root problem, and students practice discernment, noticing what passes and what remains, as the way to loosen it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five afflictions, the kleshas. Ignorance, I-ness, attraction, aversion, clinging. Did you trace a reaction to its root? Today, the root under all the roots. Day four hundred forty-nine.

You buy a new phone and, for a week, it feels like it will make you happy forever. You get a compliment and replay it for days, as if it settled who you are. You lose an argument and feel, for a whole afternoon, like that's the permanent truth about you. None of these were lies, exactly. They were mix-ups. Something passing got treated as something lasting. Patanjali puts that kind of mix-up at the very bottom of human trouble.
screen: `A NEW PHONE: HAPPY FOREVER.` → `A COMPLIMENT: WHO I AM.` → `THE PASSING, TAKEN AS LASTING.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.4: ignorance is the field for the others, whether they are dormant, thin, interrupted or fully active. Field, kshetra, like soil. I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging all grow out of it. And they can be in four states. Dormant, asleep like seeds in winter. Thin, weakened by practice. Interrupted, pushed down for a while by a stronger feeling. Or active, in full bloom. Then sutra 2.5 defines avidya with four mix-ups. Taking the impermanent as permanent. Taking the impure as pure. Taking what brings pain as pleasant. And taking what is not the self as the self. Notice that avidya isn't an empty space where knowledge should be. Vidya means knowledge; a-vidya is its opposite, an active wrong knowing that feels completely true from the inside. The commentator Vyasa compares it to how an enemy isn't merely the absence of a friend; it's the opposite of one. And the last mix-up is the deepest: taking the body, the mind, the moods, the roles, as the self, when in Patanjali's system the self is the seer, the one who watches them. You've already practiced the remedy, in chapter one: the seer resting in itself. Here's the same truth from the other side. The trouble begins the moment the seer seems to become what it sees.
screen: `THE FIELD THE OTHERS GROW IN.` · `DORMANT, THIN, INTERRUPTED, ACTIVE.` · `FOUR MIX-UPS.` · then, large: `NOT-SELF TAKEN AS SELF.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Notice something in you that feels permanent right now: a mood, a worry, a sense of who you are today. Hold it lightly, and ask: has this always been here? Will it always be? Watch it for a few breaths, and see whether it shifts, even a little. Then notice what has been watching it the whole time, the part that saw the mood come and will see it go. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Ignorance. Avidya: not a lack of facts but a wrong knowing, taking the passing for the permanent, the painful for the pleasant, the not-self for the self.
Your line: avidya. When something today feels like forever, a mood, a win, a loss, whisper to yourself: passing. And watch what changes. Day four hundred forty-nine.

Patanjali calls ignorance the field for the other afflictions
sutra 2.4: the soil the others grow in.

options: taking the impermanent as permanent.
taking the pure as impure.
none: it's just accurate.
fork.reveal: the first mix-up in 2.5: the passing taken for the lasting. moods, wins and losses all pass.

trapdoor: what you thought: ignorance means not knowing.
what it means: a wrong knowing: the passing taken as permanent, the not-self taken as the self.

450.title: I-ness (2.6)
450.hook: the second affliction hides in one tiny Sanskrit word, iva, 'as if'
450.howItsDone: In classical yoga, asmita is loosened through discernment between the seer and the seen, and teachers often have students notice the difference between awareness and the thoughts and roles it is aware of.

segments.voice: Yesterday: avidya, ignorance, the passing taken for the permanent and the not-self taken for the self. Did you whisper passing at something that felt like forever? Today, what grows first from that soil. Day four hundred fifty.

Put on a pair of rose-tinted glasses and, after a few minutes, you stop noticing them. The world just looks rosy. Ask yourself what color the sky is, and you'll say pink, and mean it. You're not lying. You've simply forgotten there's anything between your eyes and the sky. The glasses have become part of how you see, and then, without your noticing, part of who you think you are. Sutra 2.6 is about that forgetting.
screen: `ROSE-TINTED GLASSES.` → `THE SKY IS PINK.` → `YOU FORGET THE GLASSES.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.6: drig darshana shaktyor ekatmata iva asmita. I-ness is when the seer and the instrument of seeing seem to be one self. Drig, the seer: pure awareness, the purusha you met on day four hundred thirty-one. Darshana shakti, the power of seeing, here meaning the instrument, the mind, through which the seer sees. Ekatmata, one-self-ness. And then the small, crucial word: iva, as if. They are not one. They only seem to be. Asmita comes from asmi, I am. It's the felt sense of me: this body, these thoughts, these moods, my story, all bundled together and taken to be the one who sees. Like the glasses and the eyes, fused. Notice the order of the afflictions. First the mistake, ignorance. Then, from it, the mistaken me. That me is what will want things tomorrow and fear things the day after. Asmita isn't the same as arrogance. A shy person has just as much of it as a loud one. It's the basic glue that sticks awareness to the mind's contents. You may remember the same word from chapter one, in the subtlest stage of samadhi with seed: the bare sense of I am. There it was the finest object of absorption. Here it's shown as a knot. Commentators hold the two together: the sense of I am is subtle, and it still isn't the seer.
screen: `DRIG: THE SEER. DARSHANA: THE INSTRUMENT.` · `IVA: AS IF.` · `NOT ARROGANCE: THE GLUE.` · then, large: `THE GLASSES TAKEN FOR THE EYES.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Say silently, I am. Notice what comes with it: maybe a feeling in the chest, a picture of your face, a name, a role. Now notice that you are aware of all of that. The feeling, the picture, the name, all seen. Gently ask: is the one who sees them one more thing on the list? You don't need an answer. Just let the question loosen the glue a little. The bell holds the time.
I-ness. Asmita, sutra 2.6: the seer and the mind it sees through seem to be one self. Seem, as if, iva, is the key.
Your line: asmita. Today, when you catch yourself saying I am, tired, annoyed, behind, try saying I notice, tired, annoyed, behind, and feel the gap. Day four hundred fifty.

451.title: Attraction and aversion (2.7–2.8)
451.hook: two sutras, almost mirror images, explain why the mind keeps chasing and keeps running
451.tomorrow: fear of death — even in the wise
451.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers in yoga and Vedanta lineages ask students to watch raga and dvesha in daily life, pausing before acting on a like or dislike, and the Bhagavad Gita also names them as obstacles on the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday: asmita, I-ness, the seer and the mind as if fused, like glasses forgotten on your face. Did you swap I am for I notice? Today, what that I starts doing. Day four hundred fifty-one.

You walk past a bakery and smell cinnamon rolls, and before you've decided anything, you've slowed down. Your feet know. Somewhere back in your memory is a cinnamon roll that was very, very good. Then a dentist's drill starts up somewhere down the hall, and your shoulders rise. Somewhere back in your memory is a bad afternoon in a chair. Nobody chose either reaction. They were waiting. Patanjali says exactly where they were waiting.
screen: `CINNAMON ROLLS: YOU SLOW DOWN.` → `A DENTIST'S DRILL: YOU TENSE.` → `NEITHER WAS CHOSEN.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.7: sukha anushayi ragah. Attraction follows pleasure. Sutra 2.8: duhkha anushayi dveshah. Aversion follows pain. Two very short sutras, almost mirror images. The key word is anushayi, which means following after, or resting upon. Attraction rests on the memory of pleasure. Aversion rests on the memory of pain. The commentator Vyasa says it plainly: raga is the thirst for pleasure in one who remembers pleasure, and dvesha is the resentment toward pain in one who remembers pain. So these aren't random moods. They're grooves, left by experience, that pull and push the mind in advance. Now connect them to yesterday. Who got the pleasure? Who got hurt? The I, asmita. Without a me to have pleasures and pains, attraction and aversion would have nothing to hold on to. That's one reading of why they come third and fourth on the list. In these two sutras, Patanjali doesn't call pleasure itself the affliction. A cinnamon roll is a cinnamon roll. The affliction is the grip: the way a memory decides for you, before you've looked at what's actually in front of you. Attraction narrows the world to what you want. Aversion narrows it to what you're avoiding. Either way, you see less. And notice, the two are partners. A strong like often has a matching dislike close behind it: wanting the praise, dreading the criticism. Practice doesn't erase them in a day. It thins them, as sutra 2.2 promised, one noticed grip at a time.
screen: `RAGA FOLLOWS PLEASURE.` · `DVESHA FOLLOWS PAIN.` · `GROOVES LEFT BY MEMORY.` · then, large: `THE GRIP, NOT THE ROLL.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. As you sit, notice tiny pulls and pushes. An itch you want to scratch: aversion. A thought of something nice later: attraction. A sound you wish would stop. A position you'd like to shift into. Each time, name it gently, raga or dvesha, and wait one breath before doing anything. Often the pull fades by itself. If not, act, but slowly, knowing what moved you. The bell holds the time.
Attraction and aversion. Raga follows pleasure, dvesha follows pain: the third and fourth afflictions, grooves of memory that pull and push the mind.
Your line: raga, dvesha. Today, catch one craving and one avoidance as they start, and give each a single breath before you follow it. Day four hundred fifty-one.

452.title: Fear of death — even in the wise (2.9)
452.hook: the fifth affliction runs by its own momentum, and Patanjali says it's there even in the wise
452.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras often study the five afflictions with a teacher, one sutra at a time, alongside the classical commentary. Some Hindus also keep practices that face death directly, such as remembering God's name daily and hearing scripture read at the end of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: attraction and aversion, raga and dvesha. The pull toward what was sweet, the push away from what hurt. Did you catch one of them steering a small choice? Day four hundred fifty-two.
screen: `RAGA, DVESHA — THE PULL AND THE PUSH.`

segments.voice: An elevator drops half a floor and catches itself. Everyone inside grabs the rail. The nervous intern grabs it. So does the surgeon who has stood beside a hundred deathbeds and talks about dying calmly at dinner parties. Nobody decided to grab. The hands just went. That grab is older than any opinion about death. These last days have taken four of the five afflictions one at a time: not seeing clearly, I-ness, attraction, aversion. Today the last one, and he adds a phrase that should surprise anyone who thinks study is a cure.
screen: `THE ELEVATOR DROPS.` → `EVERY HAND GRABS THE RAIL.` → `THE FIFTH AFFLICTION.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.9 calls it abhinivesha. The word carries a sense of settling into, digging in. Clinging to life, the wish to go on. Patanjali gives it two descriptions. First, svarasa-vahi: it flows by its own momentum, the way a river runs downhill without anyone pushing. Second, and this is the startling part, it is established even in the wise. Vidushah api. Even in the one who knows. The classical commentary on the sutras, traditionally credited to Vyasa, fills it in with a line every creature seems to carry: may I not stop being, may I go on. Then the commentary points at something tiny. A worm that has only just hatched already shrinks from danger. It has never died in this life. So where did it learn the fear? The commentator's answer is memory: the trace of deaths before, carried forward from earlier lives. Some modern readers hear instinct there instead. Either way, the commentary's point stands: the fear is there before any learning. Notice what Patanjali does not say. He doesn't call the fear shameful. He doesn't say smart people get over it. He puts it in the wise and leaves it there, a plain reminder that reading alone doesn't dissolve it. The next two sutras say what works on the afflictions: tracing them back to where they start, and meditation. And on an ordinary Tuesday, abhinivesha is rarely about dying. It's the grip on a job you've outgrown, an old argument, the last scroll before sleep. Small endings, and the same grab at the rail.
screen: `ABHINIVESHA — DIGGING IN.` · `IT FLOWS BY ITS OWN MOMENTUM.` · `EVEN IN THE WISE.` · `THE NEWBORN WORM ALREADY FLINCHES.` · then, large: `THE SAME GRAB, IN SMALL ENDINGS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice watches the smallest ending there is: the end of a breath. Sit comfortably and let the breath run on its own. After a few rounds, notice the bottom of the out-breath, the little pause before the next in-breath arrives. Notice whether something in you hurries to grab the next breath. No need to hold your breath or stretch the pause. Just let each out-breath finish completely, and watch the next one come by itself. If anything feels uncomfortable, breathe normally. The bell holds the time.
Fear of death. Abhinivesha, the clinging to going on, the fifth affliction, which runs by itself and stays even in the wise.
Your line: abhinivesha. Today, when something small ends, a meeting, a meal, a song, notice whether you grab at it, and let it finish anyway. Day four hundred fifty-two.

453.title: Karma and its fruit (2.12–2.14)
453.hook: action leaves a deposit, rooted in the afflictions, and it ripens as a birth, a life span and what you live through
453.howItsDone: In Hindu teaching, karma is action whose results ripen over time, in this life or a later one, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras present practice as the way to weaken the afflictions that make stored action sprout.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fear of death, abhinivesha, the clinging that runs by itself, even in the wise. Did a small ending show you the grab? Day four hundred fifty-three.

Somewhere in a kitchen drawer there is a paper packet of seeds. Tomato, maybe, bought three springs ago and forgotten. It looks like nothing. Dry, light, a little dusty. Nothing is happening in there. And yet if you tip those seeds into wet soil next week, a good number of them will wake up and become exactly what they always were going to be. Not a rose. Tomatoes. Patanjali has just named the five afflictions. Now he asks what they do over time, and his answer sounds a lot like that drawer.
screen: `A FORGOTTEN PACKET OF SEEDS.` → `NOTHING SEEMS TO HAPPEN.` → `WET SOIL, AND THEY WAKE.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.12 gives the drawer a name: karmashaya. Karma is action. Ashaya is a resting place, a container. The storehouse of action. Every deed leaves something behind, and the storehouse holds it. Patanjali says its root is the afflictions, and that it will be lived out either in this birth, the one we can see, or in one we can't. Then 2.13 says how it ripens. As long as the root is there, the stored action comes to fruit in three ways: the kind of birth you get, how long that life lasts, and what you experience in it. And 2.14 says the flavor of that fruit. Joy, if the action was meritorious. Pain, if it wasn't. Notice the picture underneath all of this. There's no judge in the sutras' account, no scorekeeper adding up points. It is closer to farming. Seeds, soil, time, harvest. The classical commentary adds a homely image: rice still in its husk can sprout, but once the husk is stripped away, or the seed is roasted, it won't come up. The afflictions are the husk. Take away not seeing clearly, take away I-ness and grasping, and the seeds in the storehouse lose the power to grow. So this isn't fatalism. It's an argument for practice. Today, the storehouse is filling quietly. The sharp reply, the patient one, the favor nobody saw. Each is a small deposit.
screen: `KARMASHAYA — THE STOREHOUSE.` · `BIRTH, LIFE SPAN, EXPERIENCE.` · `JOY OR PAIN, BY MERIT.` · `A HUSKED SEED DOESN'T SPROUT.` · then, large: `THE STOREHOUSE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice looks into the storehouse gently. Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one small thing you did yesterday, kind or unkind, it doesn't matter which. Notice what it left in you: a warmth, a tightness, a replay. That's the deposit. You don't need to judge it or fix it. Just see it clearly, the way you'd hold a seed in your palm. Then set it down and come back to the breath, which is happening now, not yesterday. The bell holds the time.
Karma and its fruit. Action leaves a deposit in the storehouse, rooted in the afflictions, and it ripens as a birth, a life span and an experience.
Your line: the storehouse. Today, before one ordinary action, a text, a reply, a purchase, picture it as a seed going into the drawer. Then choose. Day four hundred fifty-three.

screen: `DAY 453 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "TO THE DISCERNING, ALL IS SUFFERING."`

454.title: "To the discerning, all is suffering" (2.15–2.17)
454.hook: the gloomiest-sounding line in the sutras turns out to be about sensitivity, and about the pain that hasn't come yet
454.tomorrow: The purpose of the world: experience and liberation
454.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often present 2.15–2.17 as a medical outline, the illness and its cause, followed later by the cure and the remedy, and students reflect on it in study and in meditation on the difference between awareness and what it is aware of.

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma and its fruit, and your line, the storehouse. Action leaves a seed, and the afflictions are the husk that lets it sprout. Did you picture one seed going into the drawer? Day four hundred fifty-four.

An eyelash falls onto your cheek. You don't notice it all afternoon. The same eyelash lands in your eye, and suddenly you can't read, can't talk, can't think of anything else. Same eyelash. Different place. Today's sutra may be the gloomiest-sounding line in the whole book. Read fast, it sounds like Patanjali hated life. But the old commentary explains it with a picture very like this one, the eye and a tiny thread, and once you see it, the line stops sounding like despair. It starts sounding like a diagnosis.
screen: `AN EYELASH ON YOUR CHEEK.` → `THE SAME EYELASH IN YOUR EYE.` → `NOT DESPAIR. A DIAGNOSIS.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.15 says: to the discerning, all is suffering. Duhkha. The one who sees clearly, the vivekin, finds pain even in pleasure, and Patanjali gives four reasons. Change: the sweet thing is already ending. Anxiety: while you have it, you fear losing it. Impressions: it leaves a groove that wants more. And the three qualities of nature, always pulling against each other, so nothing stays settled. Then the commentary, traditionally credited to Vyasa, explains who the discerning person is. Most of us, it says, are like the rest of the body. A thread of wool lands on an arm or a leg and we feel nothing. The discerning person is like the eyeball. The same thread, and it hurts. So the line is not a mood. It's about becoming sensitive enough to feel what was always there. Then comes the turn. Sutra 2.16 is just three words in Sanskrit: heyam duhkham anagatam. The suffering not yet come is to be avoided. The past is done. The present is already being lived. Only the future is still open, and that is where practice works. And 2.17 names the cause: the joining of the seer and the seen. The pure awareness that watches, and everything it watches, mind included, tangled until awareness mistakes itself for what it sees. The commentary notices that this follows the order of medicine: the disease, its cause, the cure, the remedy. Today we have the first two.
screen: `TO THE DISCERNING, ALL IS SUFFERING.` · `THE LIMB AND THE EYEBALL.` · `AVOID THE PAIN NOT YET COME.` · `THE CAUSE: SEER JOINED TO SEEN.` · then, large: `THE SEEN AND THE SEER.`

segments.voice: Today's practice sorts the seen from the seer, just a little. Sit and let the breath settle. Notice one sensation, the weight of your hands, a sound in the room, an itch. That's the seen. Now notice that something is noticing it. You don't have to name what that is. Just feel the difference between the sound and the hearing of it. Each time a thought comes, let it join the seen, one more thing in the room, and rest as the one watching. The bell holds the time.
To the discerning, all is suffering. Not a mood but a sensitivity, like the eye that feels the thread, and a turn toward the pain that hasn't come yet.

Your line: the seen and the seer. Today, when something bothers you, say quietly, that's the seen, and notice the one who sees it. Then ask what pain you could avoid tomorrow. Day four hundred fifty-four.

455.title: The purpose of the world: experience and liberation (2.18–2.22)
455.hook: the seen world exists for the seer, for two things, experience and freedom, and it doesn't vanish when one person is done
455.howItsDone: In the Samkhya and Yoga schools, the world of nature is understood to exist for the sake of awareness, offering both experience and the chance of liberation; students study these sutras with the classical commentary and reflect on them in meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the seen and the seer. To the discerning, all is suffering, and the cause is the two tangled together. Did you catch yourself watching something that bothered you? The end of a week. Day four hundred fifty-five.

There's an old picture in the Samkhya Karika, a related text whose map of seer and seen the Yoga Sutras share. A dancer performs on a stage. She dances and dances, until the one watching has truly seen her. Then she stops, because the dance has done its work. Yesterday Patanjali named the cause of suffering: the seer and the seen, joined. You might expect him to call the seen the enemy, the trap to escape. He does something stranger. He asks what the whole show is for. And he gives it a purpose.
screen: `A DANCER ON A STAGE.` → `SHE STOPS WHEN SHE'S TRULY SEEN.` → `WHAT IS THE SHOW FOR?`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.18 describes the seen: everything that can be watched, the mountains, the body, the senses, the mind itself. Its nature is light, activity and stillness, the three qualities of nature. And its purpose is two things: experience and liberation. Bhoga and apavarga. The world is there so the seer can taste it, and so the seer can finally be free of the confusion. Both. Not one instead of the other. Then 2.20 describes the seer: pure seeing, nothing more. Though it's pure, it looks out through the ideas of the mind, and so it seems to take their color. And 2.21 is the short, bold line: the seen exists only for the seer's sake. For the seer. Then 2.22 adds something tender. When one person's purpose is done, the world doesn't disappear. It stays, because it is shared with everyone else still dancing and watching. Nobody's freedom switches the lights off for the rest of us. Now the week, from the top. Ignorance: mistaking the passing for the permanent. I-ness: mistaking the instrument for the one who sees. Attraction and aversion, the pull and the push. Fear of death, even in the wise. Then karma, the storehouse, where it all ripens. Yesterday, to the discerning, all is suffering. And today, the turn: the same world that tangles us is there for our freedom. Seven days of diagnosis, and the last one ends with a reason.
screen: `BHOGA AND APAVARGA.` · `THE SEER: PURE SEEING.` · `THE SEEN EXISTS FOR THE SEER.` · `IT STAYS FOR EVERYONE ELSE.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `FOR THE SEER.`

segments.voice: Today's practice lets the world be for you, both ways. Sit and let the breath settle. First, experience: let one sense fill up. The sounds in the room, or the light through your eyelids. Taste it fully, without grabbing. Then, freedom: notice that the sound comes and goes, and the hearing stays. Move between the two, tasting and watching, as many times as you like. The bell holds the time.
The purpose of the world. In the Yoga Sutras, the seen exists for the seer, for two things: experience and liberation.
screen: `THE PURPOSE OF THE WORLD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: for the seer. Today, pick one ordinary thing, a cup of tea, a walk to the car, and let it be fully tasted, then fully let go. Day four hundred fifty-five.

screen: `DAY 455 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK OF THE AFFLICTIONS, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: DISCERNMENT IS THE WAY.`

original.note: Sanskrit apavarga: release, liberation; paired in 2.18 with bhoga, experience.

trapdoor: what you thought: spiritual people want to escape the world.
what it means: in the Yoga Sutras the world has a job: to give the seer experience, and then freedom.

what a scholar hears: 2.18 links the three gunas (light, activity, stillness) to bhoga and apavarga; 2.21 says the seen exists for the seer; 2.22 keeps the world real for others, a point against reading yoga as world-denial.
